text: A qPCR MGB probe based eDNA assay for European freshwater pearl mussel (Margaritifera margaritifera L.)

1. Environmental (e)DNA assays are becoming increasingly used to detect rare or invasive aquatic species.2. The Critically Endangered freshwater pearl mussel Margaritifera margaritifera is undergoing range-wide reduction in population numbers and distribution.3. An eDNA assay to detect the presence of M. margaritifera was developed, based on the mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase I gene, utilizing species-specific primers, a minor groove binding (MGB) probe and quantitative (q)PCR approaches.4. The results from this pilot study demonstrated high sensitivity both in laboratory and field trials, and provide a valuable non-invasive tool for detecting M. margaritifera.

across much of the species' range recruitment is low and the distribution is fragmented resulting in demographically isolated units (Geist, 2010).
The decline in abundance has prompted conservation action under national and international legislation including the listing of M. margaritifera under Annex II and V of the Habitats Directive (92/43/ EEC) and many rivers supporting populations of M. margaritifera have been designated as Special Areas of Conservation (SAC). However, the future survival of the species relies on accurate detection of populations and monitoring of extant populations. At present, survey methods are based on visual identification and quantification of individual mussels and are consequently labour-intensive and potentially destructive (Anon, 2004). The potential destructive nature of existing survey methods could be mitigated by implementing non-destructive, non-invasive monitoring tools such as environmental (e)DNA approaches.
The use of eDNA is based on interrogating environmental samples such as soil or water for the presence of DNA of target species without the need for direct sampling of individuals, and as such represents a non-invasive sampling method well suited for rare or threatened species (Pilliod, Goldberg, Arkle, & Waits, 2013). The detection of eDNA can be based on standard PCR and visualized on gel media or by employing the more sensitive quantitative PCR (qPCR) approach (Ficetola, Miaud, Pompanon, & Taberlet, 2008;Goldberg, Pilliod, Arkle, & Waits, 2011). These eDNA approaches have successfully been used to detect fish, insect larvae, crustaceans, amphibians and mammals (Dejean et al., 2012;Gustavson et al., 2015;Jerde, Mahon, Chadderton, & Lodge, 2011;Takahara, Minamoto, Yamanaka, Doi, & Kawabata, 2012;Thomsen, Kielgast, Iversen, Møller et al., 2012: Thomsen, Kielgast, Iversen, Wiuf et al., 2012,). It can provide an efficient, high sensitivity, low cost approach and is sometimes superior to other detection methods such as visual observation or capture of target organisms (Dejean et al., 2012;Jerde et al., 2011). Stoeckle, Kuehn, and Geist (2016) reported the development of specific primers for M. margaritifera anchored in the 16S mitochondrial (mt)DNA region and successfully deployed the assay on environmental (e)DNA samples from Central Europe. However, while 16S sequences from different organisms are available in public repositories, it would be advantageous to focus on the barcode of life gene (mtDNA COI - http://www.barcodeoflife.org). Publically available repositories of COI sequences contain representatives from many more organisms than any other gene sequence repository. Access to these repositories ensures that assays based on COI sequences are species-specific and only amplify the target organism. In addition, improvements of eDNA assays by using species-specific probes with higher fidelity (e.g. minor groove binding, MGB probes) would increase the species-specificity further than using an assay based solely on species-specific primers or those also incorporating TaqMan® probes not using the MGB group (Kutyavin et al., 2000).
The aim of the present study was to develop an MGB based qPCR eDNA assay to detect the presence and relative abundances of M. margaritifera without invasive sampling. This approach may also allow the detection of previously unrecorded populations that may have densities too low for observation by traditional visual survey methods.

All DNA tissue originated from a naturally deceased individual M. margaritifera found on the bank of the River Allow, Ireland (F.I. personal observations). Total DNA was extracted from the tissue sample using the Qiagen Dneasy kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA). Extracted DNA was used as a template for assay validation and standard curves for qPCR. Species-specific primers for M. margaritifera (forward primer: 5′-TTG TTG ATT CGT GCT GAG TTA GG-3′, and reverse primer: 5′-GCA TGA GCC GTA ACA ATA ACA TTG-3′) and 5′-6-FAM labelled TaqMan® minor groove binding probe (5′-CCT GGT TCT TTG CTG GGT-3′) targeting the region within the mtDNA cytochrome oxidase I (COI) region were designed using PRIMER EXPRESS 3.0 (Applied Biosystems-Roche, Branchburg, NJ). The total amplicon size, including primers, was 83 BP. Probe and primer sequences were matched against the National Centre for Biotechnology Information (NCBI -http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) nucleotide database with BLASTn (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool) to confirm the speciesspecificity for M. margaritifera in in-silico assays. To ensure that the assay only amplified M. margaritifera, it was deployed on species commonly found in Irish freshwater environments (Salmo trutta, Salmo salar, Rutilus rutilus and Abramis brama) using conventional PCR amplification and visualization on a 1.5% agarose gel stained with SYBR® Safe -DNA Gel Stain (Life Technologies). In addition, the assay was deployed using Fast SYBR ®Green Master Mix (Applied Biosystems) based qPCR (according to the manufacturer's recommendations) on tissue samples from M. margaritifera, S. trutta, S. salar and environmental samples for melting curve analyses to ensure the species specificity of the assay. In addition, to the qPCR eDNA assay for M. margaritifera, a previously developed eDNA qPCR assay (Gustavson et al., 2015) for brown trout (S. trutta) was included as a positive control for the presence of amplifiable eDNA in water samples.

section: | edna filtering and extraction of field samples
text:
Water samples were collected in sterile 3 L PET bottles from five locations in the River Allow, a tributary to the Munster Blackwater River, and stored at -20°C until further analysis. Three of the five locations had previously been visually surveyed (locations 2-4), which confirmed the presence of live M. margaritifera (http://www.duhallowlife.com/ duhallow-life/). The two locations that had not been visually surveyed were included so that future surveys could potentially confirm the findings (see Section 3). For locations 2-4, where the presence of M. margaritifera had been confirmed, samples were collected directly below the most downstream M. margaritifera patch in each location.
Water samples were thawed in ambient temperature and 1-2 L per sample was filtered through individual 0.45 μm Whatman nitrate filters. The volume of filtrate was recorded to the nearest centilitre for each sample. Filters were subsequently dehydrated with 100% EtOH before storage at -20°C. Each filter was cut into halves (half for analysis and half for archival storage) and shredded to increase surface area for eDNA extraction using Qiagen QIAshredder (Qiagen, Valencia, CA).
Total DNA was extracted using a Qiagen DNeasy kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA). Extracted DNA was stored at -20°C until further processing.

Concentrations of eDNA were determined by qPCR using an Applied Biosystems ViiA™ 7 (Life Technologies, Inc., Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA) quantitative thermocycler. Amplification reactions for each species included: 15 μL of TaqMan® Environmental Master Mix 2.0 (Life Technologies, Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA), 3 μL of each primer (final concentration of 0.2 μM), probe (final concentration of 0.2 μM), ddH2O, and DNA template (3 μL), forming the 30 μL reaction volume. The qPCR run method used warm-up conditions of 50°C for 2 min and 95°C for 10 min, followed by 40 cycles between 95°C for 15 s and 60°C for 1 min. The standard curve for M. margaritifera was generated with quantified (NanoDrop®-1000, Thermo Scientific, Wilmington, DE) DNA extractions from a tissue sample (DNA concentrations of 122.0 pg L -1 ) using seven 10:1 serial dilutions as template for qPCR. The standard curve for M. margaritifera (y = -3.4058× + 38.238, R 2 = 0.9997, efficiency = 96.62%) was generated using a 3 μL DNA template in a total reaction volume of 30 μL. All field samples were quantified in duplicate (two technical replicates), to ensure consistency, with two laboratory negative controls and M. margaritifera. Three water samples from the River Allow were used as template for S. trutta qPCR to validate the presence of amplifiable eDNA. The average Cq across technical replicates (n = 2) was used for quantification.

The present study successfully developed and deployed an eDNA assay with very high sensitivity for detecting M. margaritifera DNA in water samples. The lowest detectable concentrations of DNA (dynamic range) was 0.122 pg L -1 in the standard curves at Cq (quantification cycle) 34.8 (average over three technical replicates, SD = 0.073). No amplification was detected in any of the negative controls in either conventional PCR or in the qPCR MGB based assay. Furthermore, no cross-species (S. trutta, S. salar, R. rutilus and A. brama) amplification was present when deploying the assay using conventional PCR visualized on agarose. In addition, SYBR ®Green melting curve analyses of amplicons indicated that environmental sample amplicons had the same nucleotide composition as tissue samples of M. margaritifera, further supporting the conclusion that environmental samples contained M. margaritifera DNA.
All field samples analysed in this pilot study yielded detectable eDNA (with Cqs within the dynamic range) for both M. margaritifera and S. trutta. The presence of both M. margaritifera and S. trutta eDNA indicates that amplifiable target eDNA was present in all water samples. Resulting Cq values from the qPCR assays were transformed to pg DNA L -1 (based on the standard curve, Figure 1). The eDNA concentrations (over two technical replicates) ranged from 0.568 pg L -1 in location 1 to the highest of 33.825 pg L -1 in location 4 (Figure 2). Agreement between eDNA concentration and previously reported numbers of M. margaritifera was evident. The two locations (locations 2 and 4) with the highest count of M. margaritifera also had the highest eDNA concentrations, while the lowest number of M. margaritifera were observed in location 3, which also showed the lowest eDNA concentration (Table 1). However, although location 2 had the highest visual counts of M. margaritifera, eDNA analyses of water from the same location did not result in the highest DNA concentrations. The discrepancy between M. margaritifera counts and resulting DNA concentration could be an effect of sampling. Margaritifera margaritifera are not distributed evenly in discrete groups, but show patchy distribution on micro-geographical scales (i.e. within the river). Sampling close to a patch might result in higher DNA concentrations than sampling further away from a patch containing more individuals. While not being the focus of the current study, it is evident that specific location of samples will have an influence on resulting DNA concentrations and that there is a need to assess how different sampling approaches affect DNA concentrations. Nevertheless, the results presented here, indicate that an eDNA assay can detect the presence of M. margaritifera and with further development it may be feasible to use eDNA as a proxy for estimating M. margaritifera abundance. Accordingly, it is predicted that locations that have not been surveyed visually (location 1 and 5), could have low and intermediate counts of M. margaritifera, respectively. However, further field samples (biological replicates) and more stringent analyses (increased number of technical replicates) would be needed to allow more rigorous statements about M. margaritifera in the River Allow to be made. In addition, the assay should be a useful tool for detecting and monitoring M. margaritifera populations, and might be able to detect biomass changes and other demographic parameters (e.g. larval pulses).
In conclusion, the eDNA assay developed here can be used for rapid detection of M. margaritifera presence without the need for extensive visual surveys. Wide-scale deployment of the assay can help detect cryptic populations in catchments where M. margaritifera has not previously been reported or where M. margaritifera are considered to have become extinct.
